title: Sadhu
hookLine: one word, three times, after a gift: what is the whole room agreeing to?
tomorrow: what were the Buddha's last words, and why those?

lines: WHY THREE? WHY A HOLY MAN?
cards: Crowds have their chants: a name shouted three times, a clap that builds.

In a Lao or Thai temple, after the monks finish a blessing, or after a family hands over a gift of food or robes, the whole room answers with one word, three times: sadhu, sadhu, sadhu. Two odd things here.
Why three times? And why does the same word, in India, name a wandering holy man with ash on his skin? Same word, a temple hall and a roadside.

teach.b: Start with the meaning. Sadhu: good. Well done.

teach.h: A HOLY MAN: A GOOD ONE.
teach.b: In the discourses, the Buddha sometimes says it himself to a disciple who has answered well: sadhu, sadhu, good, good.

In Sanskrit and Hindi the same word also names a holy wanderer, and you can hear why: a sadhu is a good one, someone who has given things up. Same root of meaning, two lives. That's the first puzzle solved.
Now, what is the room agreeing to? When a family gives a meal to the monks and the room says sadhu, the people saying it didn't cook. They're rejoicing in someone else's good.
The tradition has a word for that, anumodana, and it rests on one of the twenty words from a few days ago: mudita, gladness at another's good.

Saying sadhu turns somebody else's generosity into a joy the whole room can share, and teachers say rejoicing like that is itself a good act. Now the three. Here the old texts are quiet; they don't explain it.

teach.h: THREE: THE RHYTHM OF THE CHANTS.
teach.b: What's clear is the rhythm: the homage is chanted three times, the refuges a second time and a third.
Sadhu falls into the same step. Good, good, good. Once to hear it, twice to mean it, three times to share it, as some put it.

how: In Theravada temples, people say sadhu three times, often with palms joined, after a Dhamma talk, a blessing, or an offering to the monks; some also say it on hearing of a good deed.

o: good, well done: said to rejoice in a good act
goodbye, said by monks at the end of an alms round
peace, said as a greeting when entering a temple

p: a holy wanderer: a good one
the rhythm of homage and refuges

s: sadhu is a word only monks may say
the whole room says it, after a teaching, a blessing or a gift.
in the discourses, the Buddha himself sometimes says sadhu
to a disciple who answers well: sadhu, sadhu, good, good.
the old texts explain why it's said three times
they're quiet on it. the three matches the rhythm of the chants: homage three times, refuges a second and third time.

games.q: your cousin, the one you've always been compared to, gets into her dream school. you didn't apply anywhere yet. what does sadhu point to?
o: say congrats, and mean it: her good is yours to rejoice in.
hold off until you have good news of your own.
congratulate her, but mention it was mostly luck.
games.why: sadhu is anumodana, rejoicing in someone else's good. the joy is open to anyone who says it, whoever did the deed.

practice: Bring to mind three good things other people did this week, small ones: a held door, a kind text, a meal someone made. For each, say sadhu once, quietly.
Then sit, and let yourself be glad they happened, even though none of them was yours.

wordCard.voice: Sadhu: good, well done. Said three times after a teaching or a gift, to share in someone else's good.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: sadhu, good, well done; the same letters spell the Sanskrit word.

carryVoice: Keep this one: sadhu, sadhu, sadhu, for somebody else's good, and a share of the joy. Twenty-five days of Pali.

sources.ref: sadhu: 'good, virtuous; well, very well' (also an exclamation of approval)
